Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Minh was forty-six years old, a firefighter in a midwestern city, but for two years in his late thirties he had worked as a civilian relief coordinator in a conflict zone that had no name he could say aloud anymore. The memory that held him was not a single story—it was a jumble of images he could not arrange in order no matter how many times he tried. He knew what had happened, but when he sat in the therapist’s office and opened his mouth, the words would not come. What he could feel was a sharp, familiar pain in his left shin, exactly where a piece of shrapnel had caught him as he ran toward a collapsed school. The pain returned every time the memory surfaced, as if his body were still there.

The day that undid him began with an explosion. He had been distributing food from the back of a truck when a mortar round hit a nearby market. The bang—a sound like the world cracking open—sent him diving behind crates. In the silence that followed, he heard shouts, then something worse: men laughing. When he peered out, he saw two armed men pulling a woman from a doorway by her hair, while others rummaged through the supplies he had just unloaded. Later, at the makeshift clinic, a medic made a crude comment about what had happened to the woman, and Minh had said nothing. He did not stop them. He did not intervene. He just stood there, holding a bag of rice.

Back home, the world refused to feel safe. Silence itself became a threat: the quiet between calls at the fire station made his chest tighten, because silence in the war zone had always meant something terrible was about to follow. He had come to believe that his life was destroyed—not just damaged, but erased. The man he had been before, the one who believed in helping others, had done something that went against everything he valued: he had been a witness and done nothing. He now belonged nowhere. Not with the men at the station, who told jokes he could not laugh at. Not with his wife, who eventually left after he stopped being able to speak to her at all. Not even with himself.

To manage the feelings that surged without warning—shame, guilt, a hot anger that could erupt over a misplaced tool or a rookie’s careless attitude—he developed habits that made sense only to him. When the images pressed in, he would retreat to the station bathroom and press his knuckles into the wall until the pain pushed the memory aside. Physical hurting became a release, a way to anchor himself in the present. At night, lying alone in his apartment, he performed silent mental rituals: counting backward from a hundred in three languages, repeating the same phrase until the tension in his jaw eased, because some part of him believed that if he did not do these things, another explosion would come—not in the world, but inside his own mind. He tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, but the thoughts slipped through like smoke.

At work, triggers followed him. A firework backfiring at a Fourth of July parade sent him to his knees behind the engine, heart pounding. A colleague’s offhand joke about “getting raped by the schedule” made him walk off the rig without a word, trembling. And when he saw people misbehaving—a driver yelling at a paramedic, a captain bending a rule—the moral violation he felt was so acute it was physical, as if his own integrity were being ripped open again. The irritability cost him. He had been on the job for six years, but recently his crew had started giving him space, a careful distance that only confirmed his belief that he no longer fit.

He came in for help after an incident three weeks ago. A minor argument over who should restock the hose—a small thing, trivial—and he had slammed a locker door so hard the hinge broke, then locked himself in the bunk room and cut his forearm with a razor he kept in his bag. The chief told him he had to see someone, and Minh agreed, not because he thought therapy could fix him—nothing could fix him—but because he was tired of the silence. What frightened him most was the possibility that the therapist would ask him to describe what happened, and he would sit there, mouth open, pain in his leg, and find no words at all. He hoped, barely, that maybe if someone else could speak the story for him, he might finally understand the order it would not give him on its own.
